name: KPMG
_README: Every hex below is TIER 1: read out of a file KPMG itself serves, not recalled and not
taken from a colour aggregator. The decisive source is a KPMG-hosted stylesheet whose
own first line reads '/* KPMG 2022 brand colours - CM Updated 2022-10-03 */', recovered
via web.archive.org and byte-identical across snapshots from 2023-02 to 2024-12, with
every one of its values still present in the CSS kpmg.com served on 2026-08-08.
THE TRAP THIS FILE EXISTS TO AVOID: KPMG changed its palette in 2022, and essentially
every colour-aggregator site on the internet still serves the SUPERSEDED pre-2022 values
(#005EB8 medium blue, #0091DA light blue, #483698 violet, #C6007E pink). Those values
return zero hits in KPMG's live stylesheet. A deck built from a colour-picker site is an
off-brand deck that will look subtly wrong next to real KPMG material and nobody will be
What is NOT here, because it is genuinely not public: CMYK and Pantone for the current
palette. KPMG publishes those only behind the SSO-gated Brand Central portal. The single
solid Pantone fact is KPMG Blue = Pantone 287 C -- and do NOT round-trip it, because
Pantone's own sRGB rendering of 287 C is about #003087, not #00338D. Screen work uses the
hex; print work needs the real portal.
_theme_colors_rationale: dk1/lt1 are the primary text/background pair that the slide master maps tx1/bg1 onto.
dk1 is Gray 1 #333333 because that is KPMG's live --text-color token, NOT black and NOT
KPMG Blue. dk2/lt2 hold the secondary pair: Dark blue #0C233C is the dark ground (the
single most-used token in KPMG's stylesheet, 204 occurrences) and #F5F6FA is the
off-white surface. Note #0C233C, not #00338D, is the correct dark ground -- using the
logo blue as a background is a common and visible error.
accent1-6 are ordered to match the chart series order observed in three KPMG-authored
reports from Dec 2025 to Feb 2026: KPMG Blue, Cobalt, Pacific blue, Purple, Light purple.
Because OOXML consumes accent slots in order for chart series, that ordering means a
native chart comes out in KPMG's own sequence with no further configuration.
_roles_rationale: The semantic layer components actually speak. Two rules encoded here that the raw palette
does not tell you, both from KPMG's own published guidance and measured usage:
1. Headlines on a light ground are KPMG Blue #00338D -- not the body grey, not black.
On a dark ground they are white.
2. BODY TEXT ON A LIGHT GROUND IS KPMG BLUE #00338D, NOT GREY. This inverts what an
earlier version of this file said, and the earlier version was wrong. It reasoned
from the live --text-color:#333 token, which is the WEB body colour. In KPMG's
print and deck material the body copy is set in the master blue: 19,680 characters
of it measured in a single 2025 report, against #000000 in the equivalent 2022
document. Setting long-form body text in KPMG Blue is a current-era signature and
one of the cheapest ways to make a page read as KPMG. #333333 is retained as
'ink_web' for anything genuinely screen-UI.
RE-CLASSIFIED 2026-08-09: THREE OF THESE ARE NOT DEVIATIONS, THEY ARE COMPLIANCE. The FY22
book closes with an accessibility appendix (pp.126-136) that this file previously said did
not exist. It prints per-colour WCAG tables, and on three of the four positions below it
returns the identical ratio we computed independently, with its own Fail verdict:
Gray 3 #989898   -> KPMG prints 2.88:1, Fail / Fail / Fail (p.131). Never a type colour.
Nav    #B2B2B2   -> KPMG prints 2.12:1, Fail / Fail / Fail (p.131), including the
graphical-objects column a nav tab falls under.
Cobalt on dark   -> KPMG prints 2.35:1 Fail, TWICE (p.132, p.134), and p.68's approved
list for a Dark Blue ground is White and Light Blue only. Light Blue
on Dark Blue is 12.08:1. Our substitution IS the book's prescription.
KPMG's conformance level is AA; AAA appears nowhere in 137 pages. So the wording below,
which frames these as departures from KPMG's judgment, overstates the disagreement -- we
reached the same verdicts from the same arithmetic before seeing their tables.
ONE GENUINE DEVIATION SURVIVES, AND IT IS THE REPLACEMENT VALUE RATHER THAN THE REJECTION.
#666666 passes on ratio (5.74:1) but is not a sanctioned type colour anywhere in the book;
KPMG's own muted-text answer is Gray 1 #333333 (12.63:1, named for body copy on p.64). Our
reason for #666666 is projector distance, which the book is silent on -- so that one is ours
and should be argued as ours, not as compliance.
DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM KPMG'S OWN PALETTE, and the only one in this file. KPMG uses
Gray 3 #989898 for muted text and chart axis labels. Measured against white it is
2.88:1, which fails WCAG AA at EVERY size -- the large-text threshold is 3.0. So the
'faint' role is mapped to Gray 2 #666666 (5.74:1) instead, and #989898 is used only for
non-text marks. Source lines and page numbers set in #989898 would be illegible from the
back of a large room, and a source line nobody can read is not a source line.
'on_dark_accent' is Light blue #ACEAFF rather than Cobalt, because Cobalt on Dark blue
measures 2.35:1 and is illegal at any size. The single easiest palette mistake to make is
putting a mid blue on the dark ground; the accent has to invert to a light tint.
THREE ROLES ADDED 2026-08-08 after measuring 95 rendered pages, each correcting a named
tell rather than adding a preference:
rule_strong #B2B2B2 -- the COLUMN DIVIDER and nav separator colour. 'rule' #E5E5E5 is
the CHART TRACK and only that. The two are near enough to look interchangeable in
code and are not: swapping them is one of the fastest ways a page reads as almost-
KPMG. 32 measured instances of a 0.5pt #B2B2B2 vertical divider.
chart_default #00B8F5 -- Pacific is KPMG's DEFAULT single-series bar fill, by frequency
across the corpus: #00B8F5 (116) > #1E49E2 (78) > #FFFFFF (50) > #00338D (31). Our
bar_chart reached for ctx.accent (Cobalt), which is the second choice, not the first.
nav_inactive #666666 -- KPMG's own inactive nav tab is #B2B2B2 (D1/D2; D3/D4 use
#333333), and #B2B2B2 on white measures 2.12:1. That is the SAME defect, for the same
reason, as the #989898 -> #666666 deviation documented above: a value chosen for 8pt
type in a PDF read at a desk, reused at projector distance. So the same deviation is
taken, and recorded in the same place. On a colour panel the nav inverts to #ACEAFF
(5.66:1 on Cobalt) rather than staying grey -- the accent inverts on colour, always.
cover_window_far #102C6E is the FAR STOP of the cover window's own gradient, measured
on the Global Tech Report 2026 and Pulse of Fintech covers -- the only two in the corpus
with no photograph. It is a role rather than a literal in deck.cover() for one reason: a
hex that exists only in code cannot be checked, and verify.check_deck flags any colour not
in the brand as off-palette. Making it a role is what turns a warning into a fact.
canvas_alt #F5F6FA IS RETAINED BUT SHOULD NOT BE REACHED FOR. It does not appear in the
top-28 flat colours on any of 95 pages, and across 320 pages of ten decks it measures
1.20% with no page where it is demonstrably the deliberate ground rather than a light-grey
chart fill. The real light neutral in this system is #E5E5E5, and the real ground is white.
Kept as a role because removing it would break callers; demoted in practice by every
archetype now defaulting to Ground.LIGHT.
THE SEVEN 'pair_*' ROLES ADDED 2026-08-09 are a SET, not seven independent preferences,
and that is why they are named as a family rather than folded into the roles above. KPMG's
brand book builds its covers and section dividers out of TWO colours -- a narrow vertical
element against a wide field -- and prints the complete permutation table twice (p.115
'Color combinations' and p.60 'An overview of our colors'), with one instruction: 'under no
circumstances can the same color be used twice in one layout'. Six of the seven hexes are
already in this file under other roles; #510DBC and #B497FF were dataviz-only until now.
Duplicating a hex across roles is this file's existing pattern (ink, headline and
canvas_brand are all #00338D) and it is deliberate: the role says what the colour is FOR,
and 'a member of the two-colour set' is a different job from 'the brand ground'.
The set is the 2015 book's seven colours carried forward, and carrying them forward is the
genuinely uncertain step in this whole system -- KPMG changed the palette in 2022 and only
the blues survive as recognisable successors. The mapping is argued row by row, with the
rejected alternative recorded for each contested row, in palette.py's LEGACY_2015_MAPPING.
Two facts from it belong here because they are facts about the PALETTE:
- The 2015 Green slot is RETIRED with no successor. The only 2022 greens are the two in
the chart-only 'additional colours' set, which this file already says must never appear
as page furniture. A green divider would be off-brand in a way that looks deliberate.
- Pink #FD349C is NOT in the set, on the same measured evidence that removed it from the
dataviz series below: 0.01% of 57.1 million pixels across 320 pages of ten decks. A
colour that is never a field in the corpus is not a field colour.
A FOURTH DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM KPMG'S OWN GUIDANCE, same reason as the other three.
The book asks for WHITE type on these layouts without qualification. Against the 2015 hexes
that was nearly safe -- the set bottomed out at 3.11:1. Against these hexes it is not: white
on Pacific is 2.29:1 and white on Light purple is 2.38:1, both illegal at every size. So the
TYPE-BEARING field must reach 4.5:1 against white where it carries body copy and 3.0:1 where
it carries display type only, which admits Pacific and Light purple as the ELEMENT (which
carries no type and is where they are strongest) and keeps them out from under type. Five of
the seven may be a field; all seven may be an element. This is the same deviation as
#989898 -> #666666 and nav #B2B2B2 -> #666666 above, for the same reason -- a value chosen
for small type in a PDF read at a desk, reused at projector distance in a 140-person room.
palette.py computes the classification from contrast_ratio() at import rather than storing
it, so changing a hex here moves the tiers with it instead of silently invalidating them.
_chart_only_note: RESERVED FOR DATA. NOT PAGE FURNITURE. Read out of the FY22 brand guidelines p.48, where
these eight sit inside a dotted outline captioned 'for use in infographics and charts only,
and should not be used elsewhere in our system', and hardened on p.53 into a flat rule: 'the
secondary palette is reserved for data'.
THIS EXISTS BECAUSE IT CAUGHT A LIVE DEFECT. Dark Purple #510DBC was in this package's
BODY_FIELDS -- the set of colours allowed to carry white body copy -- and Deck.blocks was
therefore painting it as a full-width content block on shipped slides. It passed every gate
we had, because every gate we had asked whether a colour was ON PALETTE and none asked what
the palette said it was FOR. #B497FF was in the Group 3 pair set for the same reason.
The distinction is invisible to contrast maths and to any off-palette check, so it has to be
carried as data: a colour can be simultaneously correct, legible, and forbidden here.
Note #63EBDA. It was flagged as a missing production colour because it appears in KPMG's own
live stylesheet as the visited-link colour and a nav underline -- i.e. KPMG's own web build
uses a chart-only colour as interface furniture. The book is the rule and the site is drift;
this file follows the book. #CDDCFE, flagged alongside it, is NOT a brand colour at all --
every occurrence in that stylesheet is a focus ring or hairline token.
_dataviz_rationale: Series order observed directly in KPMG report PDFs: KPMG Blue, Cobalt, Pacific blue,
Purple, Light purple. Bars sit on #E5E5E5 tracks with #989898 axis labels -- both
observed in three separate KPMG publications, so the track-and-label convention is real
rather than inferred.
The last two entries (#098E7E dark green, #00C0AE green) come from KPMG's own extended
'additional colours for infographics and charts' set. That set is chart-only: these are
explicitly NOT brand colours and must never appear as page furniture.
#510DBC deep purple, #76D2FF light Pacific and #0096D8 were ADDED 2026-08-08: all three
were read directly out of stacked-bar fill operators (D1 p6, D3 p16), so they are in
documented use rather than inferred from a palette chip.
#FD349C pink was REMOVED. It measures 0.01% of 57.1 million pixels across 320 pages of ten
decks -- present in the brand's colour set, absent from its practice. It stays out of the
series order so a five-series chart cannot reach it by accident.
THE SERIES ORDER IS GENUINELY CONTESTED AND THIS FILE DOES NOT PRETEND OTHERWISE. Two
orders were measured, both real, on different decks:
B (D1 p6, confirmed independently by two researchers):
There is no basis to choose, so the existing order is kept and the alternative is recorded
here rather than swapped in silently. If a deck needs B, pass the series explicitly.
_font_note: CORRECTED 2026-08-09 AGAINST THE FY22 BOOK. THIS PARAGRAPH USED TO CLAIM 'ARIAL IS NOT A
FALLBACK HERE, IT IS THE FACE KPMG MANDATES FOR POWERPOINT'. That is FALSE, and it was the
justification the whole typography approach rested on, so the correction matters.
FY22 p.58 names the PowerPoint fonts explicitly, and it splits them by ROLE: KPMG Bold for
headlines, Arial for body copy, Arial Italic and Bold for support. The same split is
repeated on p.59 and in the p.63 hierarchy table. Arial appears in a HEADLINE row nowhere in
137 pages. The older 2015-era quotation this file used ('Arial is used for subheads and body
copy in PowerPoint...') actually says the same thing on close reading -- subheads and body,
not headlines -- and was misread here as blanket permission.
SO WHAT WE DO IS A DEVIATION, AND IT SHOULD BE CALLED ONE. We set display type in Arial Bold
because KPMG Bold is a proprietary cut not licensed to us, and naming a font the delivery
machine lacks re-flows every measured box on the presenting machine. The book has no fallback
rule, no substitution guidance, and nowhere acknowledges that anyone builds KPMG-branded work
without the font -- our position lives entirely in that gap, under p.63's stated licence that
the specs are 'loose guides and can be adapted as needed'. It is defensible; it is not
compliance, and a reviewer holding p.69 -- which forbids the exactly analogous move in the
digital track, 'don't use Open Sans for headlines' -- will make the connection.
The honest summary: Arial for BODY is the rule. Arial for HEADLINES is our workaround.
The 'KPMG Font' is Giorgio Sans rebadged. The load-bearing proof is that KPMG-Extralight
and GiorgioSans-Extralight appear embedded in the SAME KPMG file sharing byte-identical
hinting parameters (BlueValues [-5,0,567,572,678,683], StdHW 22, StdVW 25), reproduced
independently. A 'Giorgio is a trademark' string was cited in an earlier draft but was NOT
reproducible on re-extraction -- subsetting strips name records -- so do not cite it.
YOU CANNOT EMBED THE BRAND FACES, for a simpler reason than fsType. An earlier draft cited
OS/2 fsType = 0x0004 as enforcing it; adversarial re-measurement read THREE DIFFERENT
fsType values for the same family across three documents, which is evidence the
measurement is invalid rather than evidence of three licences -- these are subset fonts
regenerated by Distiller/InDesign, which rewrites OS/2. The real reason needs no EULA
analysis: KPMG Font and Univers for KPMG are proprietary cuts not licensed to us at all.
We cannot embed them because we do not have them.
DATING RISK, and it is the sharpest fact on this axis: the display weight flipped from
Extralight to Bold between 2019 and 2023. KPMG documents up to 2019 embed KPMG-Extralight
with nothing bolder; every document from 2023-10 onward embeds KPMG-Bold and no light
weight at all. A deck built to the 2019 spec -- hairline display type -- will look a decade
old. This package sets display type BOLD for that reason.
Never name a typeface the delivery machine lacks. PowerPoint substitutes silently, and a
substituted face has different advance widths, so every text box measured against the
declared font re-flows -- reintroducing exactly the overflow the measurement layer exists
to prevent, and doing it on the presenting machine rather than the building one.

legal.entity_affiliation: a member firm of the KPMG global organization of independent member firms affiliated with KPMG International Limited, a private English company limited by guarantee

legal.trademark_line: The KPMG name and logo are trademarks used under license by the independent member firms of the KPMG global organization.

_legal_note: SUPERSEDED WORDING, and using it is a real compliance error rather than a style slip:
'KPMG International Cooperative ("KPMG International"), a Swiss entity'. That form was
still appearing in KPMG's own decks as late as July 2020. KPMG International Limited was
incorporated 2020-02-20 (UK company number 12474966) and the affiliation sentence above is
{member_firm} and {firm_form} vary BY MEMBER FIRM and must not be guessed. Measured
examples: 'KPMG LLP, a Delaware limited liability partnership' (US); 'KPMG Phoomchai
Business Advisory Ltd., a Thai limited liability company' (Thailand). Get the exact pair
from the firm whose deck this is.
brand_line capitalisation genuinely DISAGREES between member firms -- KPMG UK sets
'Difference', KPMG US sets 'difference'. Do not silently pick one.
Everything in this block is used ONLY in licensed mode. In the default safe mode none of
it is emitted, because a third party asserting KPMG's copyright over its own material is
worse than omitting the line entirely.

footer_geometry_pt._comment: Measured on a 960x540pt slide from two KPMG decks that agree to sub-point precision. Points from the slide's top-left. Used in licensed mode.

measured_type_scale_pt._comment: What KPMG's own decks actually use, read from content streams. NOTE the body figure: 11-14pt is DOCUMENT density, correct for a deck that is read at a desk and much too small for a 140-person room. This package's own scale keeps a 14pt floor and a 20pt body for that reason -- a deliberate, stated deviation.

RESOLVED 2026-08-09, and this line used to say the opposite. It read 'any published KPMG accessibility or contrast standard -- none found in public material'. FALSE: the FY22 brand guidelines (March 2022, obtained in full) close with an accessibility appendix -- WCAG guidance plus per-colour compliance tables for KPMG Blue, White, Cobalt, Light Blue, Dark Blue, Black and Gray 1. So KPMG does publish one, the three contrast deviations recorded above are smaller departures than they were logged as, and those tables have NOT yet been read against our roles. That reconciliation is open work
Whether tints/shades of brand colours are permitted (KPMG supplies discrete named variants instead, which reads as: use the named colour)

notes: Colour is T1 and solid. Typography is not yet established. Treat this as a strong public-source reconstruction, not as the official brand kit -- see provenance.official_source.
